Tattoo ink can remain in the skin for decades as immune cells repeatedly fail to break it down.

Once injected, the pigment draws macrophages, which absorb but cannot digest it. When they die, they release the ink, and new cells repeat the process. This keeps tattoos visible and may cause ongoing low-level inflammation.

Some particles travel to lymph nodes. Emerging research suggests ink buildup may affect immune function and the effectiveness of some vaccines, including mRNA vaccines. Inks may also contain nickel and cobalt. Alongside chronic inflammation, these have been linked to a modestly higher risk of lymphoma and skin cancer.

[Nielsen, C., Jerkeman, M., & Jöud, A. S. (2024). Tattoos as a risk factor for systemic lymphoma: A population-based case-control study. eClinicalMedicine]
